newsitem.title: FRANCE: Confident French left says Chirac must share power.
newsitem.headline: Confident French left says Chirac must share power.

text.p: French leftist leaders, brushing off a last-minute plea to voters from conservative President Jacques Chirac, called on him to share power after next Sunday's second round of a snap parliamentary election.
Socialist Party leader Lionel Jospin, the left's candidate for prime minister, said power-sharing or cohabitation "shows respect for what the people have decided."
Cohabitation "is nothing but an attitude, a type of behaviour, a spirit of responsibility towards one's country," Jospin said on Radio Luxembourg.
Socialist President Francois Mitterrand twice had to "cohabit" with centre-right governments after the left lost its parliamentary majority.
Communist Party leader Robert Hue said voter trends were moving in the left's favour after its first-round success.
"The dynamic of the first round was that many French people discovered that the left can win, and I believe that this dynamic will grow," he said on Radio Monte Carlo.
Seeking to lure back disenchanted voters, Chirac had said in a brief televised message on Tuesday that he had heard their message but urged them not to return to "the socialist ideas of yesteryear".
But the left and many commentators dismissed his appeal as too little too late, saying it had fallen short of the dramatic gesture needed to give his government a new lease on life.
"Is that all there is?" headlined the daily France-Soir over a picture of Chirac in a Superman costume.
"Chirac to the French people: "I did not understand you," trumpeted the Communist daily L'Humanite.
"Chirac's unobtainable elan: Already braced for cohabitation," said the centre-left daily Liberation.
Only the pro-government Le Figaro touted Chirac's statement, saying he had breathed new life into the majority.
French presidents typically try to remain above everyday politics but Chirac was obliged to intervene as leader of the government's campaign after forcing Prime Minister Alain Juppe to quit.
Juppe was set to attend his last cabinet meeting as premier on Wednesday, two days after promising to stand aside.
At stake for Chirac is a friendly parliament for the final five years of his seven-year presidential term.

His gamble of dissolving the National Assembly, with its strong centre-right majority, and holding an election nearly 10 months early to strengthen his hand as France heads into European monetary union, has already gone badly wrong.
"Let us take care not to compromise everything at the moment when we are reaping the first fruits of our efforts," the Gaullist president said in his televised speech.
But Hue, speaking on Radio Monte Carlo, said the "fruits" consisted of "continuing unemployment, economic uncertainty, difficulties and privatisations".
"The French people no longer want these fruits," he said.
Chirac also gave no hint of who he would choose to succeed Juppe if the ruling centre-right coalition remains in power.
Intense jockeying has broken out between socially-minded Gaullist Philippe Seguin and free-marketeering ex-prime minister Edouard Balladur for the right to succeed Juppe.

Chirac's statement, and the reaction to it, were expected to have little impact on French financial markets. Stocks were expected to rise in morning trading, unfettered by earlier worries over a possible win by the left.
